AI isn't in its dot-com moment yet.

ARK Invest's Brett Winton says AI infrastructure still isn't getting enough funding despite high yields, because investors doubt the end demand

"In the dot-com era, it's kind of like everybody was worth a gazillion dollars, no matter the metrics underneath. I think there will be a point in this cycle where that happens here, but we're clearly not there yet."

"Before you can get to that state, you need everybody who has the contrary state to basically get fired or bankrupted. And we're not there yet."

"Imagine a fixed income manager, and they have some poor guy who is trying to invest in compute attached debt or chip attached debt, and the guy is saying, these things are dynamite. These are screaming yield producing buys that we should invest in."

"He has to convince his own internal team that he should get more resources. And they're saying, well, where's the end demand? And so, even though the yields are very high, he's not getting the resources that he should."

"And that takes time. It takes at least a few years. And so, as a result, you could have these extra normal returns in the AI infrastructure space."

Micropayments get easier when AI agents can spend without asking

ARK Invest's Brett Winton on why AI agents will almost inevitably need digital assets

"Previously, the difference between free and 5 cents was like an infinite difference in terms of your ability to actually get somebody to do something, because the cognitive burden of spending 5 cents is too high for the end user."

"But if the agent is sitting there with a balance of money that it can spend as it sees fit to provide you with what you need, that could be data, an incremental service."

"The agent's ability to do that frictionlessly means they have to have a pool of assets under their control, rather than having to go back to you for approval every time."

"You probably want to stage those assets in a way where you have a big pool of assets that's protected from the agent, where it needs permission, and a smaller pool that it can wrangle. And so then almost inevitably those have to be digital assets."

text:
That tracks with my experience. I've written 4 non-fiction books with my wife (who graduated summa cum laude with a degree in journalism) acting as primary editor.

The first thing she ever edited for me was a piece that Barron's published in 1992. I—having been the Editor-in-Chief of my High School newspaper and a long-time writer—thought the version I gave to her only needed a bit of polishing. 

What came back from her was a SEA of red ink with innumerable corrections and rewrites. 

I was livid! Not only was my ego crushed, I turned it into a huge fight with her, accusing her of trying to drain all of my wonderfully creative darlings out of the piece and replacing them with pedestrian prose for the sake of clarity. The fight got so heated we ended up not speaking about it for the rest of the day.

But then I dutifully went through my original draft and made all of the changes she recommended and the scales fell from eyes—her edited version of my original draft was VASTLY better than my draft. I immediately confessed this to her while simultaneously begging her to be the primary editor on the first book I wrote called "Invest Like the Best."

In hindsight, this was the best thing that could have ever happened to my writing career. Yes, I was emotionally wounded by the harsh criticism, but it was clearly needed. I'm of the opinion that ALL writers, no matter how gifted, could see their work materially improved by a gifted, honest to the point of inflicting emotional damage

Over this period, Japanese investors have sold a cumulative -$22.0 billion in foreign long-term debt securities.

Furthermore, the group sold -$1.0 billion in overseas short-term bonds in the week ending October 17th, marking their 2nd weekly sale over the last 3.

Year-to-date, sales of foreign debt by Japanese investors are up to -$33.0 billion, the largest outflow over the comparable period since 2022.

Meet your future haggle bot

ARK Invest's Brett Winton on how AI agents could turn every consumer into an enterprise-grade negotiator

"Imagine you sign up for broadband and you agree to a price, and then periodically they bump up the price, and you're like, I guess that's the new price. If you went back to them and haggled, you would get a different price."

"You would say, listen, I'm going to leave, I'm going to switch to Spectrum instead of Frontier and Frontier will be like, oh, I forgot to tell you. We have this special deal now."

"You can imagine having an agent that's your haggle bot, trying to keep you efficient on your spend."

"It'll make a lot of businesses skate a lot thinner, because the consumer basically becomes enterprise-grade in terms of not accepting the off-the-shelf pricing in any circumstance."

Elon Musk's 2-sided compute strategy: rent to rivals, build for Grok.

ARK Invest's Brett Winton on SpaceX's surprise 13-gigawatt compute target, and how it's pulling the AI industry forward

"I anticipated that they, who had guided to like 5 to 10 gigawatts of compute by the end of '27, would be like, yeah, maybe 4 to 5 is where we're headed."

"Instead, they said, actually, we're going to get up to 13 gigawatts by the end of '27, and we have enough power and cooling available that we could get to 20."

"They're contracting out their data centers on short-term contracts rather than having to line up a long-term contract against their build."

"He's both empowering his rival, but also building up the resource he needs to catch up to his rival."

name: Chamath Palihapitiya
zh_summary: Chamath更多關於數據中心建設的想法：德克薩斯州礦產權豁免更難更長，尤其西德克薩斯。東德克薩斯除非新雲並承擔法律風險否則不可建；超大規模是最後手段。電力管道堵塞，公用事業不堪重負，真正玩家需更早更高資本承諾。建造者缺乏提供地方激勵的權力；建造者/承購者同一時更好，對資金充裕的IG超大規模有利。消費者對數據中心的反彈仍在上升。
en_summary: Chamath more thoughts on data center buildout: Texas mineral rights waivers harder and longer, especially West Texas. East Texas not buildable unless neocloud taking legal risk; hyperscalers last resort. Power pipeline clogged, utilities overwhelmed, higher capital commitments earlier for real players. Builders lack authority for local incentives; better when builder/offtaker same, benefit for well-funded IG hyperscaler. Consumer pushback rising against data centers.
ko_summary: Chamath의 데이터 센터 구축에 대한 추가 생각: 텍사스 광물권 면제가 더 어렵고 오래 걸리며, 특히 서부 텍사스. 동부 텍사스는 신클라우드가 법적 위험을 감수하지 않는 한 건설 불가; 하이퍼스케일러는 최후의 수단. 전력 파이프라인이 막혀 있고 유틸리티가 압도되며, 실제 플레이어에게 더 이른 높은 자본 약속. 빌더는 지역 인센티브를 제공할 경제적 권한이 없음; 빌더/오프테이커가 같을 때 더 나으고, 잘 자금이 조달된 IG 하이퍼스케일러에 이점. 데이터 센터에 대한 소비자 반발 증가.
text:
Some more thoughts:

1. In Texas, getting mineral rights waivers are harder and take longer than ever. Case law is useful but it’s even more critical than ever to have these in place especially in West Texas where there is lots of activity. 

2. East Texas is not buildable unless you’re a neocloud and can take the legal risk. Hyperscalers or foundational model companies may capitulate and come here but it will be a last resort type of thing. 

3. Power pipeline is clogged everywhere. Utilities are completely overwhelmed and will ratchet their pipelining process to flush out the squatters. This will mean higher capital commitments earlier in the process for those that are real. 

4.  Builders don’t have the economic authority to offer local incentives to get the utility to move them up in the queue. The ultimate offtaker isn’t as aggressive as they should be to accelerate grid connections. When the builder/offtaker is the same, these conditions get much better. This is a big benefit for being a well funded IG hyperscaler. 

5. Consumer pushback is still ratcheting up. Data centers are an easy target against the oligarchy who, collectively, still haven’t done enough to win society to their side.

text:
A bank hack would be far worse than a crypto exchange hack.

ARK Invest's Brett Winton says a bank hack could freeze the financial system, showing why holding Bitcoin could pay off

"If a major crypto exchange got hacked in a profound way, literally the assets could be transferred onchain to somebody else, and then somebody else owns them. Big problem."

"On the other hand, it's kind of a simple problem. Somebody else has the private keys. These are effectively bearer instruments."

"If somebody goes into a bank, they wouldn't necessarily be able to take the money. But they could totally scramble the accounts of the bank in a way where it would actually be a much bigger problem for the financial system if we didn't know where the money was."

"Who owes money to who suddenly gets called into question, and it would totally freeze the local financial ecosystem, and depending on the size of the bank could severely arrest the global financial ecosystem."

"In those circumstances, if you have Bitcoin or any crypto asset that is digitally secured, you'd be like, well, at least I know I have this. I do think it's illustrative of the potential option value of the asset."

ticker_notes.RKLB: Piper projects Neutron launches for AST

zh_summary: $ASTS 可能在 2027 年預訂 13 次火箭發射、2031 年達 32 次，僅八次 Falcon 9 與兩次 New Glenn 即可在 2027 年搭載約 40 顆 BlueBird 衛星，接近關鍵市場持續覆蓋所需的約 45 顆。儘管透過 Starlink Mobile 直接競爭，$SPCX 到 2031 年仍可能佔其發射的一半。替代發射商至關重要，Piper 預計 $RKLB Neutron 從 2028 年一次 AST 發射增至 2030 年每年四次。
en_summary: $ASTS could book 13 rocket launches in 2027 and 32 by 2031, with eight Falcon 9 and two New Glenn potentially carrying ~40 BlueBird satellites in 2027, nearing the ~45 needed for continuous coverage in key markets. $SPCX could still account for half its launches by 2031 despite competing via Starlink Mobile. Alternative providers matter, with Piper projecting $RKLB Neutron from one AST launch in 2028 to four annually by 2030.
ko_summary: $ASTS는 2027년에 13회, 2031년까지 32회의 로켓 발사를 예약할 수 있으며, 단 8회의 Falcon 9와 2회의 New Glenn으로 2027년에 약 40개의 BlueBird 위성을 탑재해 주요 시장 지속 커버리지에 필요한 약 45개에 가까워질 수 있다. Starlink Mobile을 통한 직접 경쟁에도 불구하고 $SPCX는 2031년까지 발사의 절반을 차지할 수 있다. 대체 발사 업체가 중요하며, Piper는 $RKLB Neutron이 2028년 AST 발사 1회에서 2030년 연간 4회로 늘어날 것으로 전망한다.
text:
$ASTS could book 13 rocket launches in 2027 and 32 by 2031 with just eight Falcon 9 and two New Glenn flights potentially carrying ~40 BlueBird satellites in 2027.

That could bring ASTS much closer to the ~45 satellites needed for continuous coverage in key markets but whats really interesting is that $SPCX could still account for half its launches by 2031 despite competing directly through Starlink Mobile.

That makes having alternative launch providers huge with Piper projecting $RKLB Neutron could go from one AST launch in 2028 to four annually by 2030 as Rocket Lab becomes another potential option for expanding the constellation.

ticker_notes.BE: turbines lose cost edge, long lead times

zh_summary: @StockSavvyShay：$BE 故事中被忽視的部分是燃氣渦輪機正在失去成本優勢，到 2030 年成本預計上升約 3.5 倍至每千瓦 3000 美元，而 Bloom 燃料電池約 3900 美元/千瓦。渦輪機交貨期長達 7 年，Bloom 可直接在資料中心發電而無需等待電網。$NVDA CEO Jensen Huang 估計 1GW AI 工廠每年可產生約 400 億美元，因此三個月延遲可能損失約 100 億美元營收，使更快獲得電力的價值遠超前期節省。
en_summary: @StockSavvyShay: Overlooked part of $BE story is gas turbines losing cost advantage, costs rising ~3.5x to $3,000/kW by 2030 while Bloom fuel cell ~$3,900/kW. Turbine lead times up to 7 years, Bloom can power data centers without grid wait. $NVDA Jensen Huang estimates 1GW AI factory ~$40B annually, so 3-month delay ~$10B lost revenue, making faster power worth more than upfront savings.
ko_summary: @StockSavvyShay: $BE 스토리에서 간과된 부분은 가스 터빈이 비용 우위를 잃고 있으며, 2030년까지 비용이 약 3.5배 상승해 kW당 3000달러에 이르는 반면 Bloom 연료전지는 약 3900달러/kW이다. 터빈 리드타임은 7년까지 늘어나고, Bloom은 그리드 연결을 기다리지 않고 데이터센터에서 직접 전력을 생산할 수 있다. $NVDA CEO Jensen Huang은 1GW AI 공장이 연간 약 400억 달러를 창출할 것으로 추정하므로 3개월 지연은 약 100억 달러 매출 손실을 의미하며, 더 빠른 전력 확보가 초기 비용 절감보다 가치가 크다.
text:
I think one of most overlooked parts of the $BE story is how quickly gas turbines are losing their cost advantage with costs projected to rise ~3.5x to $3,000/kW by 2030 while Bloom's fuel cell pricing reaches ~$3,900/kW.

That gap becomes even more interesting when turbine lead times are stretching as long as 7 years and Bloom can generate power directly at data centers without waiting on traditional grid connections.

And when $NVDA CEO Jensen Huang estimates a 1 GW AI factory could generate ~$40B annually then even a three-month delay could mean ~$10B in lost revenue which is why getting power online faster could be worth far more than saving on upfront equipment costs.

zh_summary: 相當瘋狂，GPU現在是AI供應鏈中唯一平衡的部分，而DRAM、SSD、硬碟和晶片基板面臨比正常長2-5倍的交貨時間。這意味著即使$AMZN、$MSFT、$GOOGL和$META確保了他們的$NVDA GPU，他們仍然需要CPU、記憶體和像ABF這樣的封裝材料，這些可能需要近一年才能採購，而正常只需三個月。這對$MU和$SKHY在DRAM和HBM、$SNDK在企業SSD、$WDC和$STX在硬碟以及$INTC和$AMD在CPU方面是巨大機會，因為AI代理推動整個基礎設施堆疊的需求。
en_summary: Pretty wild that GPUs are now the only balanced part of the AI supply chain while DRAM, SSDs, hard drives and chip substrates face lead times 2–5x longer than normal. That means even if $AMZN, $MSFT, $GOOGL and $META secure their $NVDA GPUs, they still need CPUs, memory and packaging materials like ABF that can take nearly a year to source versus just three months normally. That's a massive opportunity for $MU and $SKHY in DRAM and HBM, $SNDK in enterprise SSDs, $WDC and $STX in hard drives and $INTC and $AMD in CPUs as AI agents drive demand across entire infrastructure stack.

text:
Lose 10% of your trading capital and you still have 90% of your capital working for you to get back to your equity peak. You just need an 11% return to get back to even.

Lose 80% and you're trying to rebuild with only 20 cents of every original dollar. You’re destroyed. 

Drawdowns don't just take your money. They take away the capital needed to make back your losses. 

Avoid big drawdowns above all else to stay in the game.

text:
Few things:

- $SIVE is targeting T1 hyperscaler deployments for pluggables, CPO, NPO. Not quite sure what you mean by Tier 2. 

They have direct engagements with hyperscalers but currently are more upstream by qualifying with companies like Ayar, $JBL, $GFS, O-Net that eventually likely ends up -> $AMZN / $MSFT for example. 

On financing: 

- Colo players like $CIFR still need $1B+ of financing for their sites.
- Neoclouds like $CRWV need billions of financing to buy GPUs.

Higher rates + less support for financing makes it more challenging for these players. 

$SIVE already raised 700M SEK for their buildout and largely rely on external foundries, so they don't have financing constraints. 

There's pressure on players that need currently need financing for capex, but markets group up everyone in AI sector indiscriminately. 

The second nuance is whether or not this effects the end customers in terms of demand. 

I'd argue optical sector is insulated, even if overall AI capex from hyperscalers decreases, I see optical content still rising and aggregate demand rising. 

And this is especially the case with new incoming players going through their first qual cycles.

The people actually building the AI infrastructure are describing incredible demand and a multi-year supply shortage. The market is worrying about a bubble.  

$AMZN CEO Andy Jassy: Even with $220B in 2026 capex, Amazon is still leaving meaningful demand on the table. 2026 sold out. 2027 largely sold out. Good chunk of 2028 already booked.  

$SPCX CEO Elon Musk: Demand is overwhelming supply. New compute is paying back in under a year. Shortage will last a long time. Power and construction are the real bottlenecks.  

$NVDA CEO Jensen Huang: Neocloud demand is “off the charts.” Orders keep coming. Bottlenecks keep shifting (chips → packaging → HBM → power) and will last for years. The missing piece is capital, not demand.  

Stocks are down because of financing stress, higher rates and FCF optics - not because utilisation, backlog or rental pricing collapsed.   

When operators with the best visibility are still constrained and sold out well into 2027–28, the recent selloff looks more like a positioning reset than a demand air-pocket.  

This is usually when the better opportunities show up. Remember the adage "Buy fear, sell euphoria."

text: Even if AI discovered these solutions today, it would take about 7-10 years to produce sufficient evidence they solve anything in humans. It’s going to speed some things up, and there’s really good work being done by people to try and facilitate that - but the amount of data we’d need to generate to reduce the timeline to a few years…I’m not going to say anything is impossible but we’d need to pretty much redirect every dollar of investing on AI infrastructure towards bio. If the pace of discovery accelerates beyond what we are used to (especially in diseases and targets where causal biology is well understood), I won’t be surprised at all. Like AI creating better immunotherapies I’d say is likely. AI curing cancer by 2030 would not just be surprising it would mean something massive (entirely outside of AI) had changed.

zh_summary: 大型市場波動往往需要雙向行動，因為另一方參與者最終會平倉，儲存能量加速波動。含義不明確的灰色催化劑通過吸引對立觀點來維持這種動態，直到資本約束迫使交易。例子包括2020年3月COVID期間抄底者和波動率賣方助長進一步下跌，以及2021年1月迷因狂熱中GameStop和AMC的空頭為上漲增添燃料。
en_summary: Large market moves often need two-way action because participants on the other side eventually unwind, storing energy that accelerates the move. Gray catalysts with unclear implications sustain this by attracting opposing views until capital constraints force transactions. Examples include COVID in March 2020 where dip buyers and vol sellers fueled further declines, and meme mania in January 2021 with GameStop and AMC where shorts added fuel to the surge.

By nature of being a vol trader, I’ve studied many different market crashes. Not just the common ones in the U.S., but episodes like Britain in 1720, Vienna in 1873, and the Dutch tulip mania of 1637.

There are some interesting behavioral takeaways that aren’t entirely intuitive unless you participate in markets every single day.

One of the biggest for me is that large market moves often need two-way action to develop. Behaviorally, you need participants willing to take the other side, because their eventual need to unwind can help accelerate the move. It’s almost like storing energy that gets released later. To create that dynamic, a “gray catalyst” can be particularly powerful one whose implications aren’t immediately black and white. 

Here are two examples that helped produce massive moves in opposite directions that had gray area headlines that led to that two way flow. 

COVID (March 2020): What often gets lost in the sauce is that many participants were aggressively betting against the idea that COVID would be severely disruptive. As stocks fell, they bought the dip and sold vol. When stocks kept falling and vol kept rising, some of those positions became fuel for the next leg of the move as participants were forced to unwind.

Looking back, the outcome seems obvious. In real time, the eventual scale of the disruption was far from clear. There was HOPE that it would pass quickly. Headlines about potential treatments, policy support, or a less severe impact repeatedly
